{"type":"user","message":{"role":"user","content":[{"tool_use_id":"call_00_dYYoEsKnxRZ4jYMGP3DU0390","type":"tool_result","content":"     1→<div align=\"center\">\n     2→\n     3→# RLVE: Scaling Up Reinforcement Learning for Language Models with Adaptive Verifiable Environments\n     4→  \n     5→Zhiyuan Zeng*, Hamish Ivison*, Yiping Wang*, Lifan Yuan*, Shuyue Stella Li, Zhuorui Ye, Siting Li, Jacqueline He, Runlong Zhou, Tong Chen, Chenyang Zhao, Yulia Tsvetkov, Simon Shaolei Du, Natasha Jaques, Hao Peng, Pang Wei Koh, Hannaneh Hajishirzi\n     6→</div>\n     7→\n     8→![Figure1](assets/Figure1.png)\n     9→\n    10→## 🔗 Resources\n    11→- 📄 **[Paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.07317)**\n    12→- 💾 **[Code & Data](https://github.com/Zhiyuan-Zeng/RLVE)**\n    13→- 🤗 **[Models](https://huggingface.co/collections/hamishivi/rlve)**\n    14→\n    15→If you find our work useful, please consider citing:\n    16→\n    17→```bibtex\n    18→@inproceedings{zeng2026rlve,\n    19→  title={RLVE: Scaling Up Reinforcement Learning for Language Models with Adaptive Verifiable Environments},\n    20→  author={Zeng, Zhiyuan and Ivison, Hamish and Wang, Yiping and Yuan, Lifan and Li, Shuyue Stella and Ye, Zhuorui and Li, Siting and He, Jacqueline and Zhou, Runlong and Chen, Tong and Zhao, Chenyang and Tsvetkov, Yulia and Du, Simon Shaolei and Jaques, Natasha and Peng, Hao and Koh, Pang Wei and Hajishirzi, Hannaneh},\n    21→  booktitle={International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML)},\n    22→  year={2026}\n    23→}\n    24→```\n    25→\n    26→## Bug Reports & Questions\n    27→\n    28→If you have any questions about the code or the paper, feel free to contact [Zhiyuan Zeng](https://zhiyuan-zeng.github.io/) (`zhiyuan1zeng@gmail.com` or `zyzeng@cs.washington.edu`).\n    29→\n    30→If you encounter any issues while using the code or want to report a bug, please open an issue. When reporting a problem, provide detailed information so we can assist you more effectively.\n    31→\n    32→## Setup\n    33→\n    34→Our environment setup is the same as the setup of the official [slime](https://github.com/THUDM/slime) framework. We use Docker:\n    35→\n    36→```bash\n    37→# Pull the image\n    38→docker pull slimerl/slime:v0.5.0rc0-cu126\n    39→\n    40→# Start the container\n    41→docker run -d --gpus all --ipc=host --shm-size=16g \\\n    42→  --ulimit memlock=-1 --ulimit stack=67108864 \\\n    43→  --name RLVE \\\n    44→  slimerl/slime:v0.5.0rc0-cu126 \\\n    45→  tail -f /dev/null\n    46→```\n    47→\n    48→After entering the Docker container, please follow these steps to clone the repository and install it:\n    49→\n    50→```bash\n    51→cd /root/\n    52→git clone https://github.com/Zhiyuan-Zeng/RLVE.git\n    53→cd RLVE\n    54→pip install -e .\n    55→```\n    56→\n    57→## Usage of Verifiable Environments in RLVE-Gym\n    58→\n    59→Each environment has an identifier, which you can find [here](Gym/environments/__init__.py). We take the following example:\n    60→\n    61→```python\n    62→identifier = \"Sorting\"\n    63→```\n    64→\n    65→Each environment has two classes - one for the environment itself and another for controlling the problem difficulty:\n    66→\n    67→```python\n    68→from Gym.environments import identifier2environment\n    69→from Gym.parameter_controllers import identifier2controller\n    70→\n    71→environment = identifier2environment[identifier]\n    72→controller_class = identifier2controller[identifier]\n    73→```\n    74→\n    75→Note that when creating the environment, you can specify the argument `answer_markers` to control how the answer is extracted from a model’s output during verification.\n    76→By default, it extracts the answer enclosed between `<answer>` and `</answer>`.\n    77→You can check [this example usage](slime/rollout/rm_hub/rlve_rm.py) for reference.\n    78→\n    79→When generating a problem, we specify a random seed `seed` and a problem difficulty level `d` ($d \\geq 0$):\n    80→\n    81→```python\n    82→import random\n    83→\n    84→seed = 42\n    85→\n    86→controller = controller_class()\n    87→d = 3\n    88→for _ in range(d) :\n    89→    controller.update()\n    90→\n    91→problem = environment()\n    92→parameter = random.choice(controller.get_parameter_list())\n    93→if problem.generator(seed = seed, parameter = parameter) :\n    94→    pass\n    95→else :\n    96→    problem = None\n    97→```\n    98→\n    99→Problem generation is successful when `problem` is not `None`.\n   100→\n   101→The input prompt is obtained via `problem.prompt_generator()`.  \n   102→The reward for a model output `output` is given by `problem.scorer(output)`, or you can access more detailed verification information using `problem.verifier(output)`.\n   103→\n   104→You can check [here](Gym/environment.py) for more detailed usage.\n   105→\n   106→## Model Download & Weight Conversion\n   107→\n   108→In the following, we assume you are on a node with 8 GPUs, each equipped with at least 80GB of memory.\n   109→We recommend using H100 or H200 GPUs over A100s, due to recent findings regarding floating-point precision issues observed on A100 hardware.\n   110→\n   111→We download models from Hugging Face and convert their weights from the Hugging Face format to the Megatron format:\n   112→\n   113→```bash\n tools/convert_hf_to_torch_dist.py \\\n   118→    ${MODEL_ARGS[@]} \\\n   119→    --hf-checkpoint ../Qwen2.5-7B \\\n   120→    --save ../Qwen2.5-7B_torch_dist\n   121→\n   122→# R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B\n ../DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B_torch_dist\n   129→\n   130→# DeepScaleR-1.5B\n   131→hf download agentica-org/DeepScaleR-1.5B-Preview --local-dir ../DeepScaleR-1.5B-Preview\n   132→source ../DeepScaleR-1.5B-Preview \\\n   136→    --save ../DeepScaleR-1.5B-Preview_torch_dist\n   137→\n   138→# ProRL-1.5B-v2\n   139→hf download nvidia/Nemotron-Research-Reasoning-Qwen-1.5B --revision v2 --local-dir ../Nemotron-Research-Reasoning-Qwen-1.5B-v2\n   140→source scripts/models/deepseek-r1-distill-qwen-1.5B.sh\n   141→PYTHONPATH=/root/Megatron-LM python tools/convert_hf_to_torch_dist.py \\\n   142→    ${MODEL_ARGS[@]} \\\n   143→    --hf-checkpoint ../Nemotron-Research-Reasoning-Qwen-1.5B-v2 \\\n   144→    --save ../Nemotron-Research-Reasoning-Qwen-1.5B-v2_torch_dist\n   145→\n 155→**Warning:** Please make sure the weight conversion is successful before starting any training.\n   156→Even if the conversion fails, training can still launch without a runtime error, but the model will be trained from randomly initialized weights.\n   157→\n   158→\n   159→## Reward Shaping\n   160→\n   161→By default, we use the original reward provided by each verifiable environment as the reward used in the RL algorithm.  \n   162→Many environments employ continuous reward shaping, meaning that a model output can still receive a positive reward even if its answer is not fully correct.  \n   163→We found that when the training scale is small, using a binary reward can sometimes yield slightly better results (i.e., the model output receives 1 if and only if its answer is fully correct, and 0 otherwise).  \n   164→You can switch to binary rewards by changing `--reward-key reward` to `--reward-key accuracy` in `scripts/training/[MODEL]/rlve.sh`.\n   165→\n   166→## Wandb Setup\n   167→\n   168→To use Weights & Biases (wandb), please set your wandb API key in the environment variable `WANDB_API_KEY`.  \n   169→Alternatively, you can comment out the wandb-related arguments in `WANDB_ARGS` within the training script to disable wandb.\n   170→\n   171→## Environment Scaling\n   172→\n   173→You can run our environment scaling experiments as follows:\n   174→\n We take the following example:\n\n```python\nidentifier = \"Sorting\"\n```\n\nEach environment has two classes - one for the environment itself and another for controlling the problem difficulty:\n\n```python\nfrom Gym.environments import identifier2environment\nfrom Gym.parameter_controllers import identifier2controller\n\nenvironment = identifier2environment[identifier]\ncontroller_class = identifier2controller[identifier]\n```\n\nNote that when creating the environment, you can specify the argument `answer_markers` to control how the answer is extracted from a model’s output during verification.\nBy default, it extracts the answer enclosed between `<answer>` and `</answer>`.\nYou can check [this example usage](slime/rollout/rm_hub/rlve_rm.py) for reference.\n\nWhen generating a problem, we specify a random seed `seed` and a problem difficulty level `d` ($d \\geq 0$):\n\n```python\nimport random\n\nseed = 42\n\ncontroller = controller_class()\nd = 3\nfor _ in range(d) :\n    controller.update()\n\nproblem = environment()\nparameter = random.choice(controller.get_parameter_list())\nif problem.generator(seed = seed, parameter = parameter) :\n    pass\nelse :\n    problem = None\n```\n\nProblem generation is successful when `problem` is not `None`.\n\nThe input prompt is obtained via `problem.prompt_generator()`.  \nThe reward for a model output `output` is given by `problem.scorer(output)`, or you can access more detailed verification information using `problem.verifier(output)`.\n\nYou can check [here](Gym/environment.py) for more detailed usage.\n\n## Model Download & Weight Conversion\n\nIn the following, we assume you are on a node with 8 GPUs, each verifiable environment as the reward used in the RL algorithm.  \nMany environments employ continuous reward shaping, meaning that a model output can still receive a positive reward even if its answer is not fully correct.  \nWe found that when the training scale is small, using a binary reward can sometimes yield slightly better results (i.e., the model output receives 1 if and only if its answer is fully correct, and 0 otherwise).  \nYou can switch to binary rewards by changing `--reward-key reward` to `--reward-key accuracy` in `scripts/training/[MODEL]/rlve.sh`.\n\n## Wandb within the training script to disable wandb.\n\n## Environment Scaling\n\nYou can run our environment scaling experiments as follows:\n\n```bash\n# Qwen2.5-7B-Base\nbash ---------------------------------------------------------------- #\n    #  _process\n    # ---------------------------------------------------------------- #\n    def _process(self, answer: Optional[str]) -> Optional[List[int]]:\n        \"\"\"Parse the answer string into a list of integers.\n\n        Returns None if the answer cannot be parsed or contains no integers.\n        \"\"\"\n        if answer is None:\n            return None\n\n        numbers = re.findall(r'-?\\d+', answer)\n        if not numbers:\n            return None\n\n        try:\n            parsed = [int(x) for x in numbers]\n        except (ValueError, OverflowError):\n            return None\n\n        return parsed\n\n    # ---------------------------------------------------------------- #\n    #  scorer\n    # ---------------------------------------------------------------- #\n    def scorer(self, output: str) -> float:\n        \"\"\"Score the model output in [-1.0, +1.0].\n\n        Scoring strategy (two-tier):\n        ----------------------------------------\n        Tier 1 – Not a valid permutation of {1..N}:\n            score = -1.0 + coverage\n            where coverage = (distinct in-range numbers) / N.\n            This yields a score in [-1.0, 0.0).  The model gets credit for\n            producing numbers that belong to the target set.\n\n        Tier 2 – Valid permutation:\n            Let k = number of distinct prefix-sum residues modulo N\n            (1 ≤ k ≤ N).\n            score = -1.0 + 2.0 * (k - 1) / (N - 1)   for N > 1,\n            score = 1.0 for N = 1.\n            This linearly maps k=1 → -1.0 and k=N → +1.0.\n        \"\"\"\n        N = self.parameter.get(\"N\", 2)\n        if N is None or N < 1:\n            N = 2\n\n        # Extract the answer portion from the raw output.\n        answer_text = self._extract_answer_from_output(output)\n        parsed = self._process(answer_text)\n\n        # --- No integers found -------------------------------------- #\n        if parsed is None or len(parsed) == 0:\n            return -1.0\n\n        # --- Take the first N entries as the candidate permutation --- #\n        candidate = parsed[:N]\n\n        # Numbers in [1, N] that appear (deduplicated)\n        in_range = [x for x in candidate if 1 <= x <= N]\n        distinct_in_range = set(in_range)\n\n        # --- Tier 1: not a full permutation ------------------------- #\n        if len(distinct_in_range) < N:\n            coverage = len(distinct_in_range) / N  # ∈ [0, 1)\n            score = -1.0 + coverage\n            return max(-1.0, min(score, 1.0))\n\n        # --- Tier 2: valid permutation → score by residue diversity - #\n        perm = candidate  # exactly N elements, all in [1,N], all distinct\n\n        if N == 1:\n            return 1.0\n\n        # Compute prefix sums modulo N\n        seen_residues = set()\n        current = 0\n        for x in perm:\n            current += x\n            seen_residues.add(current % N)\n\n        k = len(seen_residues)  # ∈ [1, N]\n        score = -1.0 + 2.0 * (k - 1) / (N - 1)\n        return max(-1.0, min(score, 1.0))\n\n    # ---------------------------------------------------------------- #\n    #  Helper: extract answer from full model output\n    # ---------------------------------------------------------------- #\n    @staticmethod\n    def _extract_answer_from_output(output: str) -> Optional[str]:\n        \"\"\"Isolate the answer portion of a full model output.\n\n        Mirrors the base-class ``processor`` logic (strips assistant prefix,\n        then looks for ``<answer>…</answer>``) so that ``scorer`` can be\n        called on raw model outputs.\n        \"\"\"\n        if output is None:\n            return None\n\n        text = output\n        # Strip everything before the assistant turn.\n        for marker in (\"Assistant:\", \"<|im_start|>assistant\"):\n            if marker in text:\n                text = text.split(marker, 1)[1]\n                break\n\n        # Try to extract content between <answer> … </answer>.\n        m = re.search(r'<answer>(.*?)</answer>', text, re.DOTALL)\n        if m:\n            return m.group(1).strip()\n\n        # Fallback: use the whole (post-assistant) text.\n        return text.strip()\n","numLines":161,"startLine":1,"totalLines":161}}}
